tasks.short: Find the wrong translation or routing entry, look up the correct codes, write the change and its back-out, get it approved, enter the codes, test calls and log the change.

steps.what: Telecom technician finds the wrong translation or routing entry from the trouble report
Telecom technician looks up the correct codes in switch documentation and records
Telecom technician writes the code change and its back-out
Network operations engineer approves the change for the maintenance window
Telecom technician checks the approved change file before loading: entries, back-out, the switch and the window
Telecom technician enters codes needed to correct the electronic switching system programming
Telecom technician makes test calls to confirm the correction
Telecom technician completes the change log entry: written by hand today; after the change filled from the loaded change, with the test outcome added by the technician

tasks.design: A configuration view of the switch ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows the current entries next to the code dictionary, so codes are looked up in one place. Changes are written in a template that checks syntax and needs a back-out before the network operations engineer approves. The technician loads only the approved change file, test-calls, and the change log entry is filled from the loaded change; the technician adds the test outcome and saves it.
tasks.previous_blocker: Codes were looked up in printed manuals, typed line by line and logged by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Switch management tools show configurations and load checked change files.
tasks.still_hard: Older switches accept only typed commands on a local terminal.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which entry change will break a customer's special routing.

reach.learn: Whether templated changes cut failed changes.

evidence.claim: Switch management tools show current configuration and load prepared change files with syntax checks.

assumptions: Boundary: from the trouble report to the change log; customer contact is outside.
Input contract: trouble reports from the help desk; code dictionary from the switch vendor; change approval by network operations; fallback is typed commands.

Finding the fault, testing and the check before loading keep their full time. s2 keeps 60 for reading the dictionary next to the entries; s3 keeps 70 because the template checks syntax and the technician still writes the change; s5 keeps 60 for loading and watching the file; s7 keeps 20 for adding the test outcome. The log entry is an ordinary save, so it needs no approval.
The engineer's approval time is outside the technician's savings.

incremental.description: Telecom technician keeps change templates current.

approvals.approved_version: The change file with back-out exactly as approved by the network operations engineer in s4 and checked by the technician in s4b, loaded once into the named switch in the approved maintenance window; any edit needs a new approval and check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly older switches that take only typed commands, so changes are entered by hand (17.4); high: newer switches that load change files (26.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read the release notes, back up the configuration, get the update approved, install the updated software, test features such as time-correlated call routing, and record the new version.

steps.what: Telecom technician reads the vendor release notes and install instructions
Telecom technician backs up the current configuration by hand
Network operations engineer approves the update for the maintenance window
Telecom technician checks before installing: the approved version, the device, the backup taken and the window
Telecom technician installs updated software and programs on the equipment
Telecom technician tests requested features such as time-correlated call routing
Telecom technician records the new software version in the equipment records

tasks.design: A release list per device type in the network management system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) shows which equipment runs which version and which updates are due. Configuration backups run automatically before each change, and the installed version is read back from the equipment into the inventory. The update itself, its approval and testing stay with people.
tasks.previous_blocker: Versions were tracked in a spreadsheet and backups taken by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Network management systems back up configurations and read software versions automatically.
tasks.still_hard: Updates on live switches carry outage risk whatever the tooling.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing to delay an update because a big customer has an event tonight.

reach.learn: Whether the release list cuts overdue updates.

evidence.claim: Network management systems back up device configurations and read installed software versions.

assumptions: Boundary: from the vendor release to the recorded version; customer notices are outside.
Input contract: releases from the vendor portal; maintenance windows set by network operations; fallback is manual backup and spreadsheet.
Installing and testing do not change.
The engineer's approval time is outside the technician's savings.
s6 is the technician's first record of the new version and keeps its full time; transferring entries into computer records is cut in sibling task 11674.
research_questions: Do devices run fewer outdated versions?

incremental.description: Telecom technician checks failed automatic backups.

approvals.approved_version: The software version and install plan exactly as approved by the network operations engineer in s3 and checked by the technician in s3b, installed once on the named device in the approved window; another version needs a new approval and check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older devices without automatic backup, so backups are still taken by hand (3.7); high: devices managed by the network management system (12.1).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Export inventory records, compare them with what is installed on site, read remarks on mismatches, decide the right value and correct the database.

steps.what: Telecom technician exports records from the inventory database
Telecom technician performs database verifications by comparing entries with what is installed
Telecom technician reads free-text remarks on mismatched records

loop.input: The free-text remark on a mismatched record.
loop.output: A category: wrong port, retired equipment, typing error or unclear.
loop.check: Only listed categories are accepted. The technician reads each remark against its category before any correction; remarks the category does not fit, and unclear ones, are handled by hand.
loop.stop: One pass per remark; unclear remarks go to the technician.
loop.why_not_simpler: Remarks are free text written by many people; keyword rules misread them.

steps.what: Telecom technician decides the correct value for each mismatch
Telecom technician checks the final update file: each record, field and new value against the decided corrections
Telecom technician corrects the inventory database: record by record today, by loading the checked update once after the change

tasks.design: A reconciliation script reads the inventory database ({OPS_SYSTEM}) and the technician's site findings directly and lists mismatches by explicit match rules. A bounded step sorts free-text remarks on mismatched records into fixed categories for the technician to confirm. The technician decides each correction, and the technician checks the update file against the decisions before it is loaded once.
tasks.previous_blocker: Records were exported to spreadsheets and compared line by line.
tasks.enabler_now: Scripts with explicit match rules compare databases; models can sort free-text remarks.
tasks.still_hard: Some mismatches need a site visit to settle.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which of two conflicting records reflects the real cabling.

ambition.what: Run the check monthly instead of once a year.

tasks.altitude: The technician decides mismatches instead of finding them.

reach.learn: Whether cleaner records free up capacity.

evidence.claim: Reconciliation scripts with explicit match rules can list mismatches between two record sets.
Language models can sort short free-text remarks into fixed categories for a person to confirm.

assumptions: Boundary: from the inventory database to corrected records; site visits are outside.
Input contract: site findings recorded by technicians on work orders; match rules set by the network planning team; fallback is spreadsheets.
Deciding corrections stays with the technician.
No customer data go into the remark step.
research_questions: How often is a remark category wrong?

already_counted.description: Telecom technician reviews the mismatch list.

incremental.description: Telecom technician keeps the match rules current.

approvals.approved_version: The update file with record, field and new value exactly as checked by the technician in s4c, loaded once into the inventory database; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: site findings on work orders are incomplete, so the script matches few records and most comparison stays by hand (41.3); high: findings complete and match rules current (55.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Agree the requested features with the customer, design the configuration, program the switch, test with the customer, write the configuration document and send it.

steps.what: Telecom technician agrees the requested features with the customer
Telecom technician designs the configuration such as hunt groups and call routing
Telecom technician prepares the switch programming for the requested features: command by command today, by filling configuration templates from the design after the change
Telecom technician checks the filled templates against the agreed features: routing, hunt groups, times and the customer's switch
Telecom technician loads the checked configuration into the switch
Telecom technician tests the features with the customer
Telecom technician writes the configuration document
Telecom technician checks the final configuration document: features, settings and the customer contact it goes to
Telecom technician sends the checked configuration document to the customer

tasks.design: Common features such as hunt groups, night routing and time-based routing are set from configuration templates in the switch management tool ({OPS_SYSTEM}), which the technician fills from the design, checks against the agreed features and loads once. The configuration document is generated from the switch's exported settings, and the technician checks it and sends it once to the customer. Agreeing features, designing and testing stay with the technician.
tasks.previous_blocker: Features were programmed command by command and documented by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Switch management tools offer feature templates and export settings.
tasks.still_hard: Unusual customer wishes fall outside the templates.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing what a customer really needs behind the feature they asked for.

reach.learn: Whether generated documents answer more questions.

evidence.claim: Switch management tools offer feature templates and export configured settings.

assumptions: Boundary: from the feature request to the document sent; billing for features is outside.
Input contract: feature requests from account managers; templates kept by the network engineering team; fallback is command-by-command programming.

Agreeing, designing, testing and both checks keep their full time. s3 keeps 60 for filling templates and handling settings outside them; s5 keeps 40 for reading the generated document; s6 keeps 30 for the send.
Customers' testing time does not change.

incremental.description: No new upkeep: checking the generated document is s5 and s5c.

approvals.approved_version: The filled feature templates exactly as checked by the technician in s3c against the agreed features, loaded once into the customer's switch; any change needs a new check.
The configuration document exactly as checked by the technician in s5c, e-mailed once to the customer contact on the feature request; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly unusual feature requests that the templates do not cover, so programming and the document stay largely by hand (5.8); high: mostly standard features (14.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The telecom technician keeps fault finding, design, installs and tests; manual look-ups, typed commands, spreadsheet checks and hand-written documents shrink.
skills_to_grow: Working with change files and templates
role.ambitious_version: A technician whose records match the network.
